newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada defense chiefs discuss Africa outlook.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada defense chiefs discuss Africa outlook.

text.p: U.S. and Canadian defence leaders on Monday discussed the changing refugee situation in Zaire and said no decision had been made on whether to send a Canadian-led international military force to central Africa.
"There is no question there is a need for humanitarian aid," Canadian Defence Minister Douglas Young said as he began talks with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry.

Young told reporters the mission for any Canadian-led humanitarian force that might go to Zaire to help perhaps 300,000 remaining Rwandan refugees would be "to assure that that aid is delivered in an environment that's fairly secure."

But even as Young and Perry met, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said in Manila that while intervention still might be needed, a recent flood of over 500,000 Rwandans from Zaire back to Rwanda had reduced the need for a large force.
Referring to earlier suggestions of a possible 10,000-strong multinational protection force in Zaire -- including 1,000 U.S. troops -- Chretien said: "I don't think we need that much at the moment."
"It might be more in the range of 1,000 or 1,500," he told a news conference after a one-day summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
Perry and Young said in Washington that no decision had been made following a meeting of military planners who discussed Zaire in Stuttgart, Germany, over the weekend.
"Whether or not we have to do something militarily in the traditional sense of peacekeeping or humanitarian aid support is difficult to tell at this point," said Young.

The Canadian minister said intelligence indicated that "there are probably about 300,000" refugees still in Zaire but that there were also signs in the last 24 hours that some were moving toward Goma in eastern Zaire where they might cross the border into Rwanda.

Perry repeated that the U.S. military already had several hundred logistics troops at Entebbe airport in Uganda, and Mombasa airport in Kenya and a small liaison team at Kigali, Rwanda, to help any humanitarian airlift to Zaire or Rwanda.

Western military leaders met in Stuttgart on Sunday to discuss scenarios for helping refugees in Zaire that ranged from sending no new troops to using a multinational force to protect the refugees if necessary.

But they did not specify how many troops might be needed under the options, which must now go to political leaders for consideration. They also did not say where a mission could be based or what its rules of engagement might be.
